analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls every child born after 2008 in a Medicare-style health program through age 23.
analysis.headline: The bill to guarantee health coverage for all American children was sent to two House committees in 2007, with 35 cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The MediKids plan would automatically enroll every child born after 2008 in a government health program modeled on Medicare, covering them from birth through age 23. Benefits would include everything Medicare covers, all required Medicaid benefits for kids, and prescription drugs, with no out-of-pocket costs for the poorest families and reduced costs for others. Families would pay a premium through their tax return, capped at 5% of income and waived for the lowest-income families, with the Treasury instructed to propose progressive tax changes to cover the program's growing cost over time.
analysis.who_benefits: Children born after 2008 would get guaranteed, comprehensive health coverage that follows them regardless of their parents' jobs, income changes, or moves between states. The roughly 9 million uninsured children named in the bill's findings would no longer fall through gaps in Medicaid and SCHIP enrollment. Low-income families would pay no premiums and no cost-sharing; families below roughly $20,535 in income per child would owe nothing at all, and no family would pay more than 5% of its income in premiums. A refundable tax credit would cap out-of-pocket costs at 5% of income for everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children born after 2008, especially uninsured ones

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2008 would be deemed enrolled in MediKids at birth, with coverage continuing until age 23, closing the gaps in Medicaid and SCHIP that leave children uninsured when families change jobs, income, or states.

The bill's findings state that more than 9 million American children are uninsured and that uninsured children receive less preventive care and have poorer health, producing lifetime costs to themselves and the economy.

Benefits would include at least everything Medicare covers, all Medicaid-required benefits for children including screening and treatment services, and prescription drugs no worse than the 2007 standard Federal Employees Health Benefits plan option.

Families below 150% of the poverty line would pay no premiums and no cost-sharing, families below 200% would get 75% of cost-sharing reduced, and families below 300% would get 50% reduced; a refundable tax credit would cap any family's cost-sharing at 5% of income.
Children could keep private, Medicaid, or SCHIP coverage instead, but MediKids would remain the automatic default whenever other insurance was lost.

States would be barred from cutting Medicaid or SCHIP eligibility or benefits for people under 23, and any state savings from children shifting to MediKids would have to be spent on improving services such as nursing home staffing and inspections.

analysis.who_pays: Families with MediKids children would pay a monthly premium collected through the tax return, based on 25% of the program's estimated per-child cost, waived below about $20,535 of income per child and capped at 5% of adjusted gross income. Because premiums cover only a quarter of per-child costs and the program grows as new cohorts are born, the Treasury would be required to propose a schedule of progressive tax increases to fund the rest, and the Treasury's general fund would cover spending before premiums arrive. Health insurers would lose the premiums of children automatically defaulted into the public program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle- and higher-income families, and insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new mandatory premium on families with children, collected through the tax code like a tax, which would be a real cost even with the low-income exemptions and the 5%-of-income cap.

Family premiums cover only 25% of estimated per-child costs, and the bill leaves the long-term financing to a Treasury report proposing future 'progressive tax changes,' meaning the largest funding decisions would be punted to a later Congress.
The general Treasury fund would front the program's spending before premium revenue arrives, adding to federal borrowing in the program's early years.
The phase-in only covers children born after 2008, so children already uninsured at enactment would get nothing from this bill; coverage for the full population of children would take years to build.

The program would use Medicare's payment methods and let the Secretary route care through coordinated-care arrangements, raising the standard objection that a large new public payer changes how doctors and hospitals are paid and could reshape children's care delivery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: near-universal children's coverage with strong protections for low-income families and a safety net that cannot be lost to a job change. The honest cost is that this is a major new entitlement whose premiums deliberately cover only a fraction of its cost, with the real financing left as an IOU to future Congresses, and children already uninsured when it passed would have waited years for help. The design is more careful than most single-payer proposals—preserving private coverage choices and requiring states to reinvest savings—but its fiscal footing was left unfinished.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to a Ways and Means health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the MediKids Health Insurance Act of 2007 on May 17, 2007, with 25 original cosponsors.
The bill gathered 35 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The same day it was introduced, the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was then referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept children's coverage as a market they could sell into, since no public default plan was created. Families and children gained nothing: the 9 million uninsured children the bill described remained in the same Medicaid and SCHIP patchwork, with its enrollment gaps, until the program's provisions could have taken effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers; uninsured children stayed uninsured

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, proposing a Medicare-style automatic enrollment program for all children born after 2008.

for.name: 35 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; its Health Subcommittee held the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action—no hearing or markup—after the bill was sent to its health subcommittee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a parallel referral the day of introduction and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: 110th Congress Democratic leadership
against.role: House majority controlling the floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Prioritized incremental children's coverage work, including SCHIP reauthorization, rather than bringing universal children's coverage to the floor; the bill never advanced past committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never reached a floor vote where a breakdown could be recorded.

industries.note: Every child born after 2008 would be automatically enrolled in the public MediKids program, with private coverage only replacing it if a family affirmatively shows equivalent insurance. That converts a large pool of children's premiums into a public entitlement, and the bill even sets payment rates for private plans serving MediKids at pre-2003 Medicare Advantage levels, which are lower than what insurers receive today.

Covering uninsured children converts unpaid emergency-room and charity care into reimbursed treatment under Medicare-style payment rules. The bill's own findings cite emergency room usage and lost productivity as costs that would decline.

Every enrolled child would be guaranteed prescription drug coverage no worse than the standard 2007 Federal Employees plan option, creating a large new covered market. Some of that volume would be paid at Medicare-based rates, which are below commercial prices.

States could see savings as children shifted from state-funded Medicaid and SCHIP into the federal program, but the bill requires states to keep their current eligibility and benefits for people under 23 and to spend any savings on improving services like nursing home staffing.
